info.name: oauth — RFC 6749 Authorization Server
info.description:
Exercises this repo's three grants (Client Credentials, Resource Owner Password Credentials, Refresh Token) plus client/user provisioning and JWKS. Mirrors the flows documented in README.md.

Run folders top to bottom (or use Collection Runner on the whole collection) — each request captures what the next one needs into collection variables (clientId, clientSecret, username, password, accessToken, refreshToken, consumedRefreshToken). Every request is independently re-runnable except where a step deliberately depends on state from an earlier one (e.g. the refresh-rotation and duplicate-username checks).

Set `baseUrl` and `adminApiKey` (matching this repo's `ADMIN_API_KEY` env var) in the collection variables before running.

item.name: 1. Complete login flow
item.description: One end-to-end run, in order: provision a client, register a user under it, log that user in, change the password, log out, then delete the account. Every request depends on the one before it — run the folder top to bottom (or the whole collection) rather than firing them individually. It uses its own `flow*` variables, so it never collides with the error-case folders below.

item.name: 5. Old password no longer works (400 invalid_grant)

request.description: Proves step 4 took effect. Note the token from step 3 is still valid — changing a password revokes nothing.

item.name: 6. Log in again with the new password

request.description: A fresh session on the new password, so the logout step below has a live refresh token to revoke.

This is logout: RFC 7009 revocation. Revoke the *refresh* token — that consumes the grant and ends the session. The access token is a self-contained JWT verified offline against the JWKS, so it keeps working until its `exp` no matter what is revoked.
The refresh token revoked a moment ago can no longer mint anything. This is what "logged out" means server-side.
Authenticated as the owning client, the same way signup was. A user belonging to another client would report 404 rather than 403, so ids cannot be probed across clients.

item.name: 10. Deleted user cannot log in (400 invalid_grant)

request.description: Closes the loop. Any refresh token the user still held is dead too — `findAccount` resolves against the real users table on every refresh, so a deleted account fails there as well.
